Using Armstrong's axioms, which rule allows deriving X arrow Z from X arrow Y and Y arrow Z?

options.misconception: confuses reflexivity with transitivity

options.text: Transitivity allows combining the two dependencies into X arrow Z.
Augmentation alone allows it by adding Y to both sides.

options.text: Union allows it by merging the right-hand sides into YZ.
options.misconception: confuses union with chaining dependencies

questions.explanation: Armstrong's axioms include reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity. Transitivity says that if X determines Y and Y determines Z, then X determines Z. Which ACID property guarantees that a transaction sees only committed changes and no partial effects of others?

options.text: Durability guarantees that a failed transaction leaves no partial writes.

Consistency guarantees that committed data survives a power failure.

Two transactions on Pipes both write diameter after reading it. Why is this schedule not conflict serializable if their operations interleave?

options.text: Because conflicting read-write operations create a cycle in the precedence graph, so no serial order is equivalent.
Because Pipes uses more than one index during the schedule.
options.misconception: confuses serialization with index usage

options.text: Because each transaction writes diameter more than once in the schedule.
options.misconception: believes repeated writes alone break serializability

options.misconception: overstates the rule: disjoint access would be fine

Interleaved reads and writes to the same item create edges in both directions, a cycle, and therefore no equivalent serial order. Two transactions that touched disjoint items would be fine.

Which condition is necessary for a deadlock to occur among concurrent transactions?

A single transaction that holds many locks but waits on nothing.
options.misconception: describes no wait cycle at all

options.text: Two transactions reading Pipes without any locks or writes.

options.text: A transaction that commits and releases all of its locks.

How does basic timestamp ordering concurrency control decide whether an operation is allowed?

options.text: It assigns timestamps and orders operations so an older transaction's operations come first, restarting violators.

options.misconception: confuses timestamp ordering with serial execution

options.text: It assigns equal timestamps to all transactions in the same batch.
options.misconception: believes timestamps cannot distinguish transactions

Transaction B reads repair_cost written by transaction A before A commits, then A aborts. What is the consequence?

options.text: B performed a lost update on repair_cost because two writes collided.
options.misconception: confuses dirty read with lost update

options.text: B's read is safe because A's write was later undone cleanly.
options.misconception: believes an uncommitted value remains valid after abort

options.text: B made a dirty read and its result is based on a value that never became committed.
B caused A to abort by reading repair_cost first.
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect in the schedule

questions.explanation: A dirty read occurs when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not committed. If that writer aborts, the value is rolled back, so the reader has used data that was never valid in the committed state. This is distinct from a lost update and is prevented by read committed or stronger isolation.
questions.hint: Reading before commit is the defining feature of a dirty read.

What is the central rule of write-ahead logging?

options.text: A log record describing a change must reach stable storage before the changed data page is written.
Data pages must be written to disk before any corresponding log record is created.
options.misconception: reverses the order of log and data writes

options.text: Every Pipes page must be written after each SELECT to keep the log current.
options.misconception: confuses reads with logged updates

options.text: No log records are needed if the database uses a buffer cache.
options.misconception: believes buffering replaces logging

After a crash, why might committed transactions need redo even though their updates followed the log?

options.text: Because the log discards committed records after every checkpoint.
options.misconception: misunderstands what checkpoints retain

options.text: Because modified pages may not have reached disk, so committed effects must be reapplied from the log.
Because Pipes is always written directly to disk at commit time.
options.misconception: describes force writing, which would remove the need for redo

options.text: Because redo reconstructs transactions that never committed as well.
options.misconception: confuses redo with undo of incomplete transactions

questions.explanation: With a no-force buffer policy, a commit makes the log durable but need not flush dirty data pages. After a crash those pages may be missing the committed update, so redo reapplies it from the log. Transactions that were uncommitted are instead undone, so redo and undo apply to different sets.
questions.hint: Committed but not yet flushed to disk is exactly the redo case.

questions.learningObjective: reason about checkpoints in a realistic database setting
questions.stem:
While designing the water authority Pipes storage for Checkpoints, this question arises:
What is the main purpose of a checkpoint in a log-based recovery system?

options.text: To permanently delete all older rows of Pipes from the database.
options.misconception: confuses checkpoints with data purging

options.text: To make every running transaction commit at exactly the same instant.
options.misconception: confuses checkpoints with global commit

options.text: To bound recovery time by flushing dirty pages and recording the active transactions.
To replace the log entirely with a fresh snapshot of the whole database.
options.misconception: believes checkpoints eliminate the log

questions.explanation: A checkpoint writes dirty buffer pages to disk and records which transactions were active, so recovery need not scan the entire history of the log. It shortens recovery time rather than deleting data, forcing commits, or discarding the log, which is still needed for changes after the checkpoint.
questions.hint: Checkpoints limit how far back recovery must look.

options.misconception: mistakenly removes the log from recovery

Under a force policy redo of committed transactions would be unnecessary, though undo of incomplete ones could still be needed.
